pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Resultant Forces

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3 Physics — Forces):** Using force arrows in diagrams, adding forces in 1 dimension, balanced and unbalanced forces (DfE expresses the resultant as 'adding forces in 1 dimension'); 'forces being needed to cause objects to ... change their speed or direction of motion'.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS2-2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-2] (the sum of the forces is the resultant; emphasis [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-2]; assessment limited to [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-2] one variable at a time).

- **Operational details:** At 11-12, a resultant (net) force is taught as the single force equivalent to all the forces acting on an object. When the forces are balanced the resultant is zero, so there is no CHANGE in motion — the object is either stationary OR moving at constant velocity; an unbalanced resultant causes acceleration in its own direction. Teach vector addition starting collinear (combine along one line) before moving to head-to-tail addition for non-collinear forces. The persistent battles are 'no resultant means it must be stationary', 'a bigger force makes it go faster' (rather than change faster), and drawing the resultant as an extra arrow added to the free-body diagram instead of the equivalent that replaces the others.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal).
bestPractices: Start collinear: combine forces along a single line (tug-of-war / number line) before introducing 2D vectors
Use head-to-tail (or parallelogram) arrow addition for non-collinear forces; never add the magnitudes as scalars unless they are along the same line
Use predict-observe-explain with cognitive conflict — especially the constant-velocity case where forces are balanced yet the object keeps moving
Stress that the resultant points in the direction of the CHANGE in motion, not necessarily the direction of motion
Show the resultant REPLACING the individual forces (the equivalent), not drawn as an additional arrow alongside them
Tie 'resultant = zero' explicitly to BOTH stationary and steady-speed cases
keyRepresentations: Free-body diagram of arrows, with the resultant shown separately as the single equivalent
Tug-of-war / number line for collinear addition
Head-to-tail vector triangle (or parallelogram) for non-collinear addition
commonMisconceptions: No resultant force means the object must be stationary (ignores constant velocity)
A bigger force makes an object go faster — conflating force with speed rather than with acceleration (rate of change)
The resultant is read as an extra/additional force acting on the body (Gunstone et al.)
The direction of the resultant equals the direction of motion (it should be the direction of CHANGE of motion)
Adding non-collinear vectors as scalars, or using a 'bisector' shortcut for the resultant direction
Motion implies a force in the direction of travel (the impetus backbone misconception)

learn.summary: For 11–12 year-olds, teach resultant (net) force as the single force equivalent to all forces on an object: a zero resultant means NO CHANGE in motion (stationary OR constant velocity), while a non-zero resultant causes acceleration in its own direction. Confront three stubborn errors — 'no resultant means stationary', 'bigger force means faster' (rather than changing motion faster), and reading the resultant as an extra arrow added to the forces rather than the equivalent that replaces them. A single force's direction is the direction of the CHANGE in motion, not automatically the direction of travel. Build vector addition collinear-first (along one line) before head-to-tail addition for non-collinear forces.

activities.title: Force-arrow playground: balanced forces that keep gliding
feedback: If you predicted the moving crate would stop when forces are balanced: balanced forces give a zero resultant, meaning no CHANGE — an already-moving object keeps its steady speed. Here friction is treated as negligible, so no other horizontal force is present to slow it.

If you expected the crate to reach a fixed fast speed and stay there while the rightward arrow stays longer: a constant unbalanced force pointing along the motion keeps accelerating the crate, so its speed keeps climbing for as long as that force acts.
If you read the resultant as an additional push: notice the overlay replaces the original arrows — it is their single combined effect, not an extra force.

For the angled case (crate starting from rest): the resultant is built head-to-tail; it is not the bisector of the two arrows, and it is not found by adding their lengths as plain numbers. Starting from rest, the crate accelerates along the resultant; if it were already moving in another direction, an angled resultant would curve its path rather than instantly align travel with the force.
activities.rationale: The decisive cases — balanced forces producing constant velocity, and a sustained unbalanced force along the motion making speed keep rising — are dynamic relationships that a live model lets the learner size arrows for and watch drive motion in real time, surfacing the 'balanced = stationary' and 'bigger force = faster' errors. A linked live resultant arrow and head-to-tail mode make the combination mechanism concrete. The model treats horizontal friction as negligible so the drawn arrows represent all horizontal forces; each prediction is tied to a stated initial motion.
sourceClaims: A zero resultant force corresponds to no change in motion — either stationary or constant velocity; an unbalanced resultant causes acceleration in its direction; the resultant points in the direction of the change of motion, not necessarily of motion.
Forces must be combined as vectors (head-to-tail or parallelogram); adding magnitudes as scalars is only valid when collinear, and the 'bisector' direction is a common error.
learnerActions: Set the crate moving steadily to the right. In this model horizontal friction is treated as negligible, so the only horizontal forces acting are the arrows you draw.
On the already-moving crate, place two equal and opposite horizontal force arrows and adjust their lengths so they are exactly balanced (zero resultant).
Predict what the already-moving crate will do BEFORE releasing: will it stop, slow down, or keep moving at the same speed? State your reasoning.
Observe the crate: with balanced forces (zero resultant) it keeps gliding to the right at a steady speed rather than stopping.

Now make the RIGHTWARD arrow longer than the leftward one, so the resultant points right — the same direction the crate is already moving — and watch it accelerate; keep that arrow stretched and notice its SPEED keeps climbing for as long as the unbalanced force acts along the motion.
View an overlay showing a single resultant arrow that REPLACES the separate arrows (not drawn in addition to them).

Switch to the non-collinear mode: this clears the previous motion and sets the crate at rest. Place two arrows at an angle, join them head-to-tail to build the resultant geometrically, then watch the crate accelerate from rest along that resultant direction.
activities.intendedInsight: A zero resultant means no change in motion — which includes continuing to move at a steady speed, not only being at rest. A sustained unbalanced resultant keeps changing the motion; when it points along the direction of travel the speed keeps climbing, showing that force governs CHANGE of motion rather than speed itself. The resultant is the single equivalent of the combined forces, and for non-collinear forces it is found by head-to-tail (vector) addition. This model assumes negligible horizontal friction, so the drawn arrows are the only horizontal forces.

activities.title: Combining forces and judging the direction of change
feedback: For 30 N right and 20 N left, the resultant is 10 N to the right — you subtract opposing magnitudes only because they lie on the same line.
For a car that is moving forwards and braking, the resultant points BACKWARDS (opposite the motion), because the motion is changing by slowing down.
If you placed the resultant along the direction of travel for a slowing object: the resultant follows the direction of CHANGE, not the direction of motion.
A zero resultant can still have several forces present — they simply cancel; it does not mean there are no forces.
activities.rationale: Retrieval through construction, direction-judgement, and categorisation rehearses the 'bigger force = faster' and 'balanced = stationary' distractors and the 'resultant along the motion' error. Recognition and multiple-choice items assess and rehearse but do not by themselves elicit the felt confrontation of balanced-yet-moving, so pair them with the hands-on model.
sourceClaims: Forces must be combined as vectors (head-to-tail or parallelogram); adding magnitudes as scalars is only valid when collinear, and the 'bisector' direction is a common error.
Common student errors include treating the net force as an additional force on the body and believing a larger force produces a greater speed rather than greater acceleration.

A zero resultant force corresponds to no change in motion — either stationary or constant velocity; an unbalanced resultant causes acceleration in its direction; the resultant points in the direction of the change of motion, not necessarily of motion.
learnerActions: Drag arrows head-to-tail (or along a number line for collinear cases) to construct the resultant, then draw or state its direction and size.
For collinear forces, calculate the resultant: e.g. 30 N right and 20 N left gives 10 N to the right.
Answer multiple-choice items on which way the resultant points for an object that is stated to be speeding up, slowing down, or turning, and justify the choice from the stated initial motion.
Categorise described situations as balanced (zero resultant, no change in motion) or unbalanced (non-zero resultant, motion changes).
Decide whether a zero resultant means there are no forces on the object, and explain.
activities.intendedInsight: Collinear forces combine by signed addition along the line; non-collinear forces need head-to-tail construction. The resultant points in the direction of the CHANGE in motion — which can be opposite to the current direction of travel when an object is slowing down. A zero resultant does not mean there are no forces; it means the forces balance.

activities.title: Tug-of-war predict–observe–explain
feedback: If you predicted 'lots of force, so it should move' or 'the stronger side's force is left over': equal and opposite pulls cancel to a zero resultant regardless of how hard each side pulls.
Skydiver at steady speed: weight down and air resistance up are equal, so the resultant is zero — yet she IS moving, at a constant speed. Zero resultant means no change, not stopped.
Braking car that is moving forwards: the resultant points backwards (opposite the forward motion) because the car is slowing down.
activities.rationale: A moving-but-steady case forces the split between 'moving' and 'changing motion', directly addressing the dominant 'zero resultant means stationary' misconception and the 'leftover force' idea. Predict-observe-explain with cognitive conflict is well suited to the constant-velocity case.
sourceClaims: A zero resultant force corresponds to no change in motion — either stationary or constant velocity; an unbalanced resultant causes acceleration in its direction; the resultant points in the direction of the change of motion, not necessarily of motion.
Common student errors include treating the net force as an additional force on the body and believing a larger force produces a greater speed rather than greater acceleration.
learnerActions: Set up two students to pull a rope tied to a central marker; they will both pull hard and adjust until the marker holds still.
Before the pulling starts, predict: if both students pull hard and the marker is held still, what is the resultant on the marker? Does a big pull on each side mean a big resultant? Say WHY.
Observe that the marker can be held still even under large pulls, then explain in terms of the resultant why, while it stays still, the two pulls must be equal and opposite.
Discuss the skydiver case: during a steady (terminal-velocity) fall, state the resultant and whether she is moving.
Discuss a braking car that is still moving forwards: state which way the resultant points and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Large equal and opposite pulls still give a zero resultant; the size of the individual forces does not add up to a 'big leftover'. A zero resultant means no change in motion, so a steadily falling skydiver has a zero resultant yet is still moving, and a forwards-moving braking car has a backward resultant while still moving forwards.

activities.title: Free-body diagram reference with the resultant as equivalent
feedback: If you drew weight, air resistance AND a separate resultant all acting at once: the resultant replaces the combined forces — show it on its own, not as an extra force.

A balanced free-body diagram (arrows cancel to a zero resultant) implies no change in motion; it does not by itself tell you whether the object is at rest or moving steadily — the skydiver at terminal velocity (weight balanced by air resistance) and a book sitting still (weight balanced by support from the table) both have zero-resultant diagrams, even though one is moving and the other is not.
activities.rationale: A static labelled diagram is a useful reference for naming forces and practising the resultant-as-equivalent idea. Because it is static it cannot itself show balanced forces producing steady motion, so it supports but does not replace the dynamic model; treat it as a reference scaffold.
sourceClaims: Common student errors include treating the net force as an additional force on the body and believing a larger force produces a greater speed rather than greater acceleration.
learnerActions: Reveal, one at a time, the labelled forces on a chosen object (e.g. a book resting on a table, or a skydiver).
Identify each force's direction and relative size from its arrow.
Reveal the resultant drawn separately as the single equivalent arrow, and confirm it is NOT added alongside the individual forces.
State what a static diagram does and does not tell you: it fixes the force balance, but a zero resultant alone does not reveal whether the object is at rest or moving steadily.
activities.intendedInsight: A free-body diagram shows all forces as arrows; the resultant is their single equivalent, drawn on its own rather than as an extra arrow among the originals. For a supported object such as a book on a table, the downward weight and the upward support from the table balance. A static snapshot shows the force balance but not, by itself, whether a zero-resultant object is stationary or moving at constant velocity.

constraints: Build vector addition collinear-first (combine along a single line, e.g. tug-of-war or number line) before head-to-tail addition for non-collinear forces.
Only add force magnitudes as plain numbers when the forces are collinear; otherwise use head-to-tail (or parallelogram) construction. The bisector of two arrows is NOT the resultant direction.

When describing speeding up, slowing down, or turning, always state the object's initial motion: the resultant sets the CHANGE in motion and may point opposite to the current direction of travel (e.g. a braking car still moving forwards). A resultant pointing along the existing motion makes the object speed up in a straight line (more generally, it speeds up whenever the resultant has a part along the motion); starting from rest it accelerates along the resultant, but an angled resultant on an already-moving object curves the path rather than instantly aligning travel with the force.
Tie 'zero resultant' explicitly to BOTH the stationary case and the constant-velocity case; never present zero resultant as meaning stopped.

In the dynamic crate model, state that horizontal friction is treated as negligible so the drawn arrows are the only horizontal forces; two balanced arrows then give a zero resultant and constant velocity. This is a stated model, not a universal requirement.

Recognition and multiple-choice items assess and rehearse but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a resultant or the felt balanced-yet-moving confrontation; pair them with hands-on construction and the dynamic model.

The static free-body diagram is a reference scaffold: being static it cannot display balanced forces producing steady motion, and a zero-resultant diagram alone does not distinguish rest from constant velocity.
3D vector work is deferred; at this stage the curriculum works in a plane and planar vectors carry resultants fully — treat 3D as later extension, not as adding conceptual content now.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the listed sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Sources in the original row are marked verified:false; evidence strength and effectiveness are not established here.

The source attributing the 'net force as an additional force' and 'bigger force = faster speed' errors is credited to Gunstone et al. / Education Victoria; original attribution retained but not re-checked.

Checked the collinear example: 30 N right minus 20 N left gives 10 N right — consistent and retained. The skydiver terminal-velocity case correctly implies a zero resultant while still moving — retained as stated.

The original crate recommendation did not state the crate's initial motion or friction model, and described the non-collinear crate as 'veering off precisely along' the resultant while already moving; these have been corrected to state the initial motion, declare a negligible-friction model, and start the non-collinear case explicitly from rest, since a resultant sets acceleration (not velocity) and only a from-rest object travels exactly along it.
The non-collinear mode is an explicit motion reset (crate placed at rest) so the from-rest claim does not silently contradict the earlier moving-right setup.

assess.poeTask: Have two students pull a rope tied to a central marker, adjusting until the marker holds still though both pull hard. Ask the class to predict the resultant on the marker, and whether a big pull on each side should mean a big resultant, and WHY, before revealing it isn't moving. Predicting 'lots of force, so it should move' or 'the stronger side's force is left over' reveals the balanced=stationary and leftover-force ideas; a standstill under large equal pulls makes a zero resultant concrete.
probeDeeper: Earlier in her fall she was speeding up. What was the resultant force then, and which way did it point?
A car brakes to a stop while still moving forwards. Which way does the resultant force point — forwards or backwards? Why?
Two people push a box: 30 N right and 20 N left. What's the resultant, and what does the box do?
If the resultant is zero, does that mean there are no forces on the object?
assess.correctAnswer: The resultant force is zero — weight down and air resistance up are equal and opposite, so they balance. She IS moving (falling fast), but at a steady speed: a zero resultant means no CHANGE in motion, which can be either stationary or constant velocity. A zero resultant does not mean stopped.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'She's moving, so the resultant can't be zero — something must be winning.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: A zero resultant means no CHANGE in motion — constant velocity counts; revisit steady-motion cases repeatedly.
errorPatterns.distractor: The resultant can't be zero — she's still falling, so weight must be winning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses a zero resultant for a moving object.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A bigger resultant force means a faster speed.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: The resultant sets the CHANGE in motion (acceleration/direction of change), not the speed; a fast object can have a zero resultant.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads a large resultant as 'going fast' rather than 'changing motion quickly'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The resultant is an EXTRA arrow you add on top of the other forces.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: The resultant REPLACES the individual forces — it's their single combined effect, drawn on its own, not added to them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws weight, air resistance AND a separate resultant all acting at once.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The resultant force always points the way the object is moving.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: The resultant points in the direction of the CHANGE in motion — e.g. backwards when the object is slowing down.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For a decelerating or turning object, draws the resultant along the motion.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks a zero resultant means stationary, or reads a bigger resultant as a bigger speed; draws the resultant as an extra arrow among the others.
responseLevels.full: Treats force as a vector, combines collinear forces into a single resultant that REPLACES them, and links a zero resultant to no change (rest or constant velocity) and a non-zero resultant to a change in the direction it points — transferring to skydiver, braking and tug scenarios.
responseLevels.partial: Calculates resultants of collinear forces and states 'balanced = no change', but can't apply it to a moving-but-steady case, or muddles the resultant's DIRECTION (points it along the motion) — rules stated, not connected to motion.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A skydiver falls and, for a while, falls at a STEADY speed (terminal velocity) — not speeding up. Two forces act on her: her weight downwards and air resistance upwards. What is the resultant force on her during this steady fall — and is she moving?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The recurring error is 'zero resultant means stationary'. A moving-but-steady case forces the split: a student who understands says the resultant is zero AND she is still moving (no change), whereas a student with the misconception either denies the resultant can be zero (because she's moving) or insists she must be stopped. It also exposes 'motion needs a net force'.
